What to Know About Fire Districts and Insurance Requirements

When buying land in Colorado—especially in rural or mountain areas—fire risk can have a major impact on your budget, insurance, and even your ability to build. Here’s what you need to know about fire districts, wildfire zones, and how to protect your property and investment.

What Is a Fire Protection District?

Fire Protection Districts (FPDs) provide fire and emergency services to rural properties that are often outside city limits. If your land is in one, you may be subject to:

  • Annual fire district fees or taxes
  • Minimum driveway width and turnaround requirements
  • Water storage or hydrant distance rules

High-Risk Wildfire Zones

Properties in designated wildfire zones may face additional requirements and higher insurance costs. These areas often require:

  • Defensible space around structures (cleared vegetation)
  • Class A roofing and non-flammable siding
  • Tree thinning or removal for fire mitigation

You can check your fire risk on county GIS maps or the Colorado Wildfire Risk Map.

Insurance companies may deny coverage or charge significantly more if you are in a high fire zone without mitigation or community fire response nearby.

How It Affects Insurance

  • Some insurers will not write new policies in certain fire zones
  • Higher premiums for homes more than 5–10 miles from a fire station
  • New builds may require fire-resistant materials to qualify

It’s essential to get insurance quotes before closing on land in fire-prone areas.

Tips for Buyers

  • Ask for a copy of the Fire District Service Plan
  • Call the local fire department to verify protection and response time
  • Budget for fire mitigation during development
